title: iPads Do Not Belong in School
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin argues that handing iPads and Chromebooks to young children in school is unjustified, and that the burden of proof should sit with the EdTech companies rather than with skeptical educators. She opens with the near-universal provision of school devices and a photo of kindergarteners using district iPads on the playground, then reverses the usual defensive posture by demanding independent evidence that screens improve learning. She notes that favourable studies are routinely funded by the vendors who benefit, and works through common justifications such as paper savings, the digital divide and the claim that tech is the future. Her alternative is what she calls tech-intentionality: later is better, less is more, relationships and skills before screens. She closes with six concrete school-level steps, including ending K-8 1:1 programs, restoring computer labs and tech teachers, disconnecting curriculum from the internet, and enforcing bell-to-bell phone bans.
points: Burden of proof: schools should have to show that devices improve learning, and most positive research traces back to industry-funded sources.
The common pro-tech arguments (easier learning, paper savings, closing the digital divide) are each rebutted, with the claim that learning depends on struggle and human relationships.
Her tech-intentional framework is later is better, less is more, relationships and skills before screens.
Practical steps include ending 1:1 programs below grade 9, bringing back shared labs and technology teachers, and teaching tech education without technology.
Savings from 1:1 programs could instead fund smaller classes and teacher support.
quotes: Of course, we know that actual use of such devices varies significantly from district to district, school to school, and even classroom to classroom. Getting an accurate quantitative measure of “time spent on iPads for Kindergarten” is difficult. But I would argue that even knowing an exact number wouldn’t make me feel better about an iPad’s presence in the Kindergarten classroom in the first place.

But it makes me angry that we’re not turning this around and asking the opposite questions: “Show me how iPads improve learning. Show me that YouTube use on a student Chromebook in a classroom benefits a child’s social skills. Show me that learning to read or write on a screen is better than with pencil and paper.

To be clear– there is plenty of “evidence” that iPads “help” learning…but dig a little deeper and you find that these “studies” are conveniently funded by the very companies who benefit from favorable findings in the first place.

Being tech-intentional™ means using screen-based technologies that enhance, nurture, and support students in a way that aligns with our values, and resisting, limiting, or delaying screen use that interferes with healthy mental, physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development. The TL;DR version is this: Later is better Less is more Relationships and skills before screens

Eliminate all 1:1 programs for K-8th grade, at a minimum. The benefits of “less is more” at younger grades especially is well-documented. The costs to implement such programs is high, as well as the costs to maintain hardware and update software. That money could be much better spent on policies and programs that reduce class size or support teachers.
